The Four Heavenly Kings and the Asuras together churned the Milk Ocean to obtain nectar; they built a palace on this mountain and guarded it for seven days before dividing it, and thus the name Rājagṛha City was established.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are also three explanations. One states:
When the King of Magadha first had a son born, he had one head, two faces, and four arms.

Later, having grown to adulthood and possessed of great power, he ruled over the world of Jambudvīpa; he took eighteen thousand kings of various nations and settled them within these five mountains, and for this reason it was named Rājagṛha (the City of the King’s Abode).
One account states:
A fire broke out in the city where King Māgadha previously resided; one house was burned down and another rebuilt, and this occurred as many as seven times.
The people of the country were exhausted by the labor, so the king immediately sought another place to dwell.
Seeing these five mountains encircling it like a city wall, he immediately constructed a palace and resided therein; thus, it was named Rājagṛha (the King’s Abode).
According to another account:

in ancient times, there was a king of this country named Mahāgovinda (Broad Chariot) who went out on a hunting expedition and encountered these five mountains, which were surrounded by steep and solid ridges and adorned with various wonders. He then abandoned his original capital and settled within them.
Because the king previously resided here, it is named Rājagṛha (the City of the King’s Abode).
The details are as explained there.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "This city is the largest; it is three hundred yojanas in length and breadth, containing eight hundred million households and eighty thousand villages."
If one were to provide a detailed analysis, it would be as found in the *Records of the Western Regions*.
The name "Gṛdhrakūṭa" is a corruption and abbreviation; the correct term is Kṣudrakūṭa, which in the language of Tang means "Vulture Peak" or "Vulture Terrace."
Since this mountain is inhabited by vultures (*gṛdhra*) and its shape resembles a high terrace, it is named after the bird.
What was formerly called "Vulture Peak" (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*), or "Vulture Ridge," or "Spiritual Vulture," all convey the same meaning.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are two interpretations of this term.
The first states:
because the summit of the mountain resembles a vulture (*gṛdhra*), it is called "Vulture Peak" (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*).
One explanation states:
Because vultures dwell upon its summit, it is named Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak).

This means that in the Śītavana (Cemetery) forest to the south of Rājagṛha, there were many corpses; vultures would constantly come to feed on them and then return to the mountain top. Consequently, people of the time came to call it Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.
Furthermore, another record states:
"Ling" refers to spiritual immortals (*xianling*).
This bird possesses such spirituality that it knows whether a person is alive or dead.
When people were about to die, it would lead them as if to their own homes;
when they waited for the corpses to be carried to the forest, the bird would fly down to eat them.
Because it could know this in advance, it was called the "Spiritual Vulture" (Gṛdhrakūṭa).
Furthermore, Paramārtha’s *Commentary on the Seven Matters* states: "The *Vinaya-vibhāṣā* says:
When Śākyamuni was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he took the body of a vulture."
His parents were old and had lost their sight; out of gratitude to repay their kindness, he sought food to provide for them as an offering.
A householder in the city of Rājagṛha entered the mountains and saw him, whereupon he asked: "What merit is there in making such offerings?"
The vulture preached the Dharma to him in accordance with the truth.
The householder was greatly delighted and said,
"You are a benevolent deity of this mountain."
"From this day forward, for the remainder of my life, I shall provide for you.
Because of this, all the birds received offerings.
The vulture said to the birds:
"You all should repay the kindness of your benefactor.
The birds did not understand his intent; day after day, they stole the property of others and sent it as provisions to the elder.
When people lost their belongings, they went to the king to lodge a complaint.
The king questioned the elder, who replied truthfully according to the facts.
Upon hearing this, the king was struck with wonder and entered the mountains, where he preached the Dharma for the vulture.
The king was greatly delighted and later sent offerings.
Because this mountain was inhabited by a numinous bird, it is named Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa).
The Sūtra states:
"Together with a great assembly of eight hundred million *koṭis* of bhikṣus."

The commentary states: From here below is the fifth section, concerning the capacities of those to be taught. Within this, there are two parts: [The first part: "Among these, there are two [types of] persons. This means that within the aforementioned three types of persons, there are further two categories. First, there are those who have already entered the path; second, there are those who have not yet entered the path. Among those who have already entered the path, there are again two categories: first, those who have already attained the fruit; second, those who have not yet attained the fruit. Among those who have not yet attained the fruit, there are again two categories: first, those who have already generated the roots of goodness; second, those who have not yet generated the roots of goodness. Among those who have not yet generated the roots of goodness, there are again two categories: first, those who have already planted the seeds of liberation; second, those who have not yet planted the seeds of liberation. Among those who have not yet planted the seeds of liberation, there are again two categories: first, those who have already encountered the conditions for liberation; second, those who have not yet encountered the conditions for liberation. Among those who have not yet encountered the conditions for liberation, there are again two categories: first, those who possess the lineage; second, those who lack the lineage. Among those who lack the lineage, there are again two categories: first, those who will eventually encounter the conditions for liberation; second, those who will never encounter the conditions for liberation. Among those who will never encounter the conditions for liberation, there are again two categories: first, those who are fixed in the wrong way; second, those who are fixed in the indeterminate state. These are the various distinctions among those who have not yet entered the path. As for those who have already entered the path, they are all included within the category of those who have already attained the fruit. Those who have already attained the fruit are of two kinds: first, those who have already realized the ultimate fruit; second, those who have not yet realized the ultimate fruit. Those who have not yet realized the ultimate fruit are of two kinds: first, those who are still training (*śaikṣa*); second, those who are no longer training (*aśaikṣa*). Those who are still training are of two kinds: first, those who have already abandoned the afflictions of the desire realm; second, those who have not yet abandoned the afflictions of the desire realm. Those who have not yet abandoned the afflictions of the form realm are of two kinds: first, those who have already abandoned the afflictions of the formless realm; second, those who have not yet abandoned the afflictions of the formless realm. Those who have not yet abandoned the afflictions of the formless realm are of two kinds: first, those who have already attained the fruit of stream-enterer; second, those who have not yet attained the fruit of stream-enterer. Those who have not yet attained the fruit of stream-enterer are of two kinds: first, those who have already attained the fruit of once-returner; second, those who have not yet attained the fruit of once-returner. Those who have not yet attained the fruit of once-returner are of two kinds: first, those who have already attained the fruit of non-returner; second, those who have not yet attained the fruit of non-returner. Those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of cultivation are of two kinds: first, those who have already attained the stage of the path of no-more-learning; second, those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of no-more-learning. Those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of cultivation are of two kinds: first, those who have already attained the stage of the path of no-more-learning; second, those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of no-more-learning. Those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of no-more-learning are of two kinds: first, those who have already attained the stage of the path of accumulation; second, those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of accumulation. Those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of accumulation are of two kinds: first, those who have already attained the stage of the path of preparation; second, those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of preparation. Those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of preparation are of two kinds: first, those who have already attained the stage of the path of application; second, those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of application. Those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of application are of two kinds: first, those who have already attained the stage of the path of seeing; second, those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of seeing. Those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of seeing are of two kinds: first, those who have already attained the stage of the path of cultivation; second, those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of cultivation. Those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of cultivation are of two kinds: first, those who have already attained the stage of the path of no-more-learning; second, those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of no-more-learning. Those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of no-more-learning are of two kinds: first, those who have already attained the stage of the path of accumulation; second, those who have not yet attained the stage of the path of accumulation.
